subtype: Stage 5: Separate, calm, listen to both [Response]
passage:
Mother's journal, Wednesday.
Ayaan (6) and Mehr (4) fought over the block tower again. Mehr knocked it down; Ayaan pushed her. Both screamed.
This time I didn't shout. I took Ayaan to the sofa and Mehr to the rug, then sat on the floor between them. I asked Ayaan first. "You wanted your tower." He nodded, tears falling. Then Mehr. "You felt scared when he pushed you." She nodded too.
In two minutes both were calm. 🤍 Ayaan offered to build another one.
— Salma

qa.q: Where did Salma take Ayaan and Mehr?
qa.a: She took Ayaan to the sofa and Mehr to the rug.

qa.q: How can you tell Ayaan felt understood?
qa.a: He nodded with tears falling when Salma said he wanted his tower, and later offered to build another one.

qa.q: Why did Salma's approach calm the fight so quickly?
qa.a: She separated them, sat at their level and named each child's feeling, so both felt heard instead of judged.

qa.q: What is it like for Mehr when Salma names her fear?
qa.a: Mehr likely feels safe and understood, which is why she nods and calms down.

grounding: It shows a parent separating the children, getting down to their level, letting each speak and naming their feelings, which cools the fight.

subtype: Stage 5: Separate, calm, listen to both [Response]
passage: Payal and Pintu were fighting in the yard behind the house, both pulling at one kite. Pintu yanked; the kite tore. Payal screamed and hit him. Indu came out from the cowshed, wiping her hands. She did not shout. She knelt on the mud, one child on each side. "Payal, tell me." "He tore it!" "You were sad your kite tore." Payal sniffed and nodded. "Pintu?" "She hit me." "That scared you." Pintu's chin wobbled. Indu held both their hands. After a while, they sat quietly, and Pintu picked up the torn kite.

qa.q: Where did Indu come out from?
qa.a: She came out from the cowshed, wiping her hands.

qa.q: What does Pintu's wobbling chin suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he felt scared and hurt, and was relieved his feeling was named.

qa.q: What did Indu do that calmed both children?
qa.a: She knelt at their level, let each one speak and named what each felt, instead of deciding who was wrong.

qa.q: How might Payal see her mother after this?
qa.a: Payal likely feels her mother listens to her, which makes her calmer and more willing to sit quietly with Pintu.

grounding: It illustrates a parent kneeling at the children's level, letting each tell what happened and naming their feelings, which cools the fight.

subtype: Stage 5: Separate, calm, listen to both [Response]
passage:
In their Lagos house, Chidi had knocked down Ada's block tower, and Ada had bitten his arm. Both were howling.

Emeka didn't shout. He knelt down between them, so his face was at their level.

"Okay. One at a time. Chidi, what happened?"

"She bit me!"

"That hurt. You were scared. Ada, what happened?"

"He broke my tower!"

"You wanted your tower. You worked hard on it."

Ada nodded, sniffing. Chidi stopped crying and looked at his arm.

"Now," Emeka said, "shall we build it again? Together?"

In two minutes, both were stacking blocks.

qa.q: What did Ada do to Chidi?
qa.a: She bit his arm.

qa.q: How did Ada feel when Emeka said "You wanted your tower"?
qa.a: She felt understood and calmer, nodding and sniffing, because her feeling had been named.

qa.q: Why did Emeka's approach work better than scolding?
qa.a: He got down to their level, let each speak, and named both feelings, so both felt heard and the fight cooled quickly.

qa.q: How did Chidi respond once Emeka named his fear?
qa.a: He stopped crying and calmed down, looking at his arm instead of shouting.

grounding: Emeka kneels between his fighting children, lets each tell what happened and names their feelings, and being heard cools the fight faster than judgement.

subtype: Stage 5: Separate, calm, listen to both [Response]
passage:
At the Kochi daycare, Sabina and her little brother Arif fought over the red tricycle until both fell and cried.

Payal, their teacher, didn't ask who started it. She sat down on the floor between them.

"Sabina, tell me what happened."

"I was riding and he pushed me!"

"You wanted to keep riding. That makes sense."

"Arif, your turn."

"She never gives it!"

"You wanted a turn, and you were tired of waiting."

Both children stopped crying and looked at Payal.

"Let's use the sand timer," she said. "Sabina first, then Arif." They both nodded.

qa.q: What were Sabina and Arif fighting over?
qa.a: The red tricycle.

qa.q: How did Arif feel when Payal said "You were tired of waiting"?
qa.a: He felt heard and calmer, and stopped crying.

qa.q: Why did Payal's approach cool the fight?
qa.a: She sat at their level, let each speak, and named both feelings without blaming, then offered a fair plan with the sand timer.

qa.q: How might Sabina feel after being listened to first?
qa.a: She probably feels understood and more willing to share after her turn.

grounding: At daycare, Payal sits with two fighting siblings, lets each explain and names their feelings, and the fight cools faster than judgement would allow.

passage:
I'm Jomon's cousin Rashmi, and I was staying with them for the holidays when I saw his mother do something I haven't forgotten.

Jomon and his little sister Anna were screaming over a toy boat in the bath. Water everywhere.

His mother knelt beside the tub. She didn't say "Who started it?" She said, "Jomon, tell me." He said Anna grabbed it. She said, "You wanted your boat." Then, "Anna, tell me." Anna said Jomon splashed her face. "You felt scared when the water hit you."

They both went quiet. Then Jomon handed Anna the boat. I couldn't believe it.

qa.q: What were Jomon and Anna fighting over?
qa.a: A toy boat in the bath.

qa.q: How did Rashmi feel watching Jomon hand Anna the boat?
qa.a: Rashmi was surprised and impressed, finding it hard to believe the fight ended so quickly.

qa.q: What did Jomon's mother do that worked?
qa.a: She knelt at their level, let each child speak, and named each feeling instead of asking who started it.

qa.q: How did Anna feel when her mother named her fear?
qa.a: She felt understood and calmer, and went quiet.

grounding: Rashmi, a cousin, observes a mother kneel, let each child speak and name their feelings, cooling a sibling fight faster than judgement.

Monday. Eshaan and Mehak fought over the tower. Papa shouted, "Stop it, both of you!" Both cried louder.
Thursday. They fought again. This time Papa knelt down between them. "One at a time. Eshaan?"
"She knocked my tower!"
"You wanted your tower to stay up." Eshaan nodded, sniffing.
"Mehak?"
"He pushed me."
"You felt scared when he pushed." Mehak hiccupped and leaned on Papa.
The next Monday. A shout came from the rug. Before Papa got there, Eshaan said, "Papa, I'm angry, she took my block!" Mehak said, "I wanted a turn." Papa sat down with them, and the fight was over in a minute.

qa.q: What did Papa say to Eshaan on Thursday?
qa.a: He said, "You wanted your tower to stay up."

qa.q: How did Mehak feel when Papa said, 'You felt scared when he pushed'?
qa.a: She felt comforted and understood, so she hiccupped and leaned on Papa instead of crying louder.

qa.q: What did Papa change between Monday and Thursday that worked?
qa.a: Instead of shouting, he knelt at their level, let each speak in turn and named their feelings, which cooled the fight quickly.

qa.q: How might Eshaan experience being listened to?
qa.a: Eshaan feels heard, and by the next Monday he can say 'I'm angry' himself instead of only fighting.

grounding: Shows a parent getting down to the children's level, letting each tell their side and naming feelings, and how being heard cools fights.
